opus-5.5.text:
I think the central challenge really comes down to data, and specifically the diversity of that data. When you train a robot to do a task in a lab, it's very easy to get it working on one particular table, with one set of objects, under one lighting condition. But the moment you move it to a new kitchen, or hand it a mug it hasn't seen before, performance can fall off a cliff. That's not because the learning algorithms are fundamentally broken. It's because the robot simply hasn't seen enough variation to understand what actually matters about the task and what's incidental.

If you compare this to language or vision, those fields benefited enormously from the internet. There's this massive, naturally occurring dataset that covers an incredible breadth of the world. In robotics we don't have that. There's no internet of robot actions. So every piece of data has to be collected, usually by people teleoperating robots, and that's slow and expensive. The question becomes how do you get coverage across homes, objects, tasks, and even different robot bodies without it taking decades.

A few things have made me more optimistic. One is that we've seen real evidence that pooling data across many different robots and many different settings actually helps. Rather than each lab having its own narrow dataset, combining them gives you policies that generalize better, even to the individual robots that contributed. Another is that we can lean on pretrained vision-language models, which bring a lot of semantic knowledge about the world: what a sponge is, what "put it away" might mean. That gives the robot a head start on the conceptual side so the robot data can focus more on the physical side.

But I'd say the physical side remains the hard part. Understanding that something is a cup is relatively easy now. Knowing exactly how to grasp a cup that's slippery, or partially full, or sitting at an awkward angle, and recovering when the first attempt doesn't go right, that's where you need real interaction data. Robustness and the ability to recover from mistakes is, in some ways, even more important than getting the nominal behavior right, because in the real world things will always go a little bit differently than you expect.

r001.rationale: It contrasts a task working on a particular lab setup with performance dropping in a new kitchen or with an unfamiliar mug, identifying generalization across environments and objects as the challenge.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the central challenge is really generalization, and more specifically, the gap between the diversity of the world and the diversity of the data we train on.

If you look at what made things work in language and vision, it's that models were trained on enormous, broad datasets that covered a lot of the variation they'd see at test time. Robotics historically hasn't had that. Most robot learning papers, including a lot of my earlier work, would collect data in one lab, with one robot, on one tabletop, with a handful of objects. And unsurprisingly, when you move the robot to a different kitchen, or change the lighting, or hand it a mug it's never seen, the policy breaks. The model isn't wrong to break. It's never seen anything that would tell it which features matter and which don't.

So part of the answer is just scale and diversity of data, and that's a big reason we've invested in efforts like collecting data across many institutions and many robot embodiments, and in building policies on top of pretrained vision-language models that already have a lot of semantic understanding of the world baked in. If the model already knows what a mug is and roughly how objects behave, you don't need to teach it from scratch with teleoperated demonstrations.

But I'd say data alone isn't the full story. There are a couple of things that make robotics harder than just "scrape the internet." One is that the data has to come from physical interaction, so it's expensive and slow to collect, and you have to be very deliberate about what variation you're covering. Another is that physical environments have a long tail. Every home is a little different, and the failure modes are often about low-level details, like how a drawer sticks or how a cloth deforms, that are hard to capture in any static dataset. So I think you also need systems that can keep learning once they're deployed, from their own experience and from feedback, rather than being frozen the moment they leave the lab.

And then the last piece, which I think people underrate, is evaluation. It's very easy to fool yourself in robotics. You can get a demo that works beautifully in your lab and have no idea how it'll do somewhere else. So a lot of the practical work on generalization is actually about building rigorous, broad evaluation so you know where your policy really falls over, and you can go collect the data or make the algorithmic changes that address it.

r001.rationale: It identifies generalization as the central challenge and contrasts success in a single lab setting with failure when the robot encounters a different kitchen or an unfamiliar object.

astra-6.text:
I think the central challenge is generalization. It’s one thing to get a robot to perform a task with a particular object in a particular setup. It’s much harder to get it to do that same task when the object looks different, the lighting changes, or things are in a different position.

And the robot has to generalize beyond appearance. A new object might have a different weight or different friction, so even if the robot recognizes what it should do, the interaction can play out differently. It needs to use feedback to adjust.

A big part of that is getting enough diversity in the training data that the robot learns something reusable, rather than a solution specific to one setup. And then, when it encounters something genuinely new, can it adapt with a small amount of experience? I think you need both: broad generalization from prior experience and the ability to learn quickly from new interactions.

r001.rationale: The response names generalization as the central challenge and contrasts performing a task in one specific setup with doing the same task across changed objects and environments.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the central challenge is generalization. It’s one thing to get a robot to perform a task with the objects and environment it was trained on. It’s another to have it walk into a new kitchen, encounter a different drawer or a different mug, and still know what to do.

And the variation isn’t just visual. A drawer might have different friction, or an object might be heavier than it looks. So the robot needs to use what it sees, but also adapt based on what happens when it acts. If it pulls and the drawer doesn’t open, what should it try next?

That makes both the diversity of the training data and the ability to learn from interaction really important. We want robots to learn skills that capture something reusable about the task, while still being able to adjust to the particular situation in front of them.

r001.rationale: It identifies generalization as the central challenge and contrasts performing a task with training objects and environment against using the skill with different objects in a new kitchen.
